Everyman. A late-medieval morality play from around 1495 in which a representative human figure is summoned by Death to account for his deeds before God.

As Everyman prepares for his judgment, he desperately seeks companions for his journey to the grave. Fellowship abandons him. So do his kinship and his cousin. When he turns to his Goods, his material wealth, they refuse him too, exposing the illusion that worldly bonds might sustain us in our darkest hour.

Even his own faculties desert him. Strength leaves him. Beauty abandons him. Discretion and the Five Wits—the senses and knowledge—all slip away at the very brink of death. Only Good Deeds remains faithful, having been nourished by his virtuous acts throughout his life.

Knowledge, however, guides Everyman to Confession, where he repents and performs penance. Through sacramental grace, Good Deeds is restored to strength and becomes his only true companion in death and his journey to heaven.

The play speaks in plain language suited to popular audiences, with each character a moral abstraction rather than a person of psychological depth. Its power lies in its existential clarity: the levelling of all ranks before death, the stripping away of all illusions, the solitary journey each soul must take alone. The work stands as the most celebrated surviving example of the morality play, canonical in English drama.
